questions.stem: Which is an example of a quality control inspection in the supply chain?
options: checking a sample of incoming raw materials against specifications
surveying customers about which new products they would like to buy
comparing the business's prices with those of its main competitors
reviewing the business's cash flow forecast at the end of each month
questions.explanation: Quality control inspections check materials, work in process or finished goods against set standards at points in the supply chain. Customer surveys are market research.

questions.stem: A Sydney clothing brand sends an inspector to its overseas supplier's factory to check garments before they are shipped. Why inspect at this point?
options: faults are found before the cost of shipping and selling defective stock
it removes the need for any further checks once the stock arrives
it guarantees that every garment produced will be free of defects
it transfers all legal responsibility for faulty goods to the customer
questions.explanation: Inspecting before dispatch catches defects early, avoiding freight costs, returns and damage to reputation. Sample inspections reduce but cannot guarantee zero defects.

questions.stem: Which is the main limitation of relying on quality control inspections in the supply chain?
options: they can be used only for services, not for manufactured goods
they find defects after resources are used, rather than preventing them
they can be carried out only by government agencies, not by businesses themselves
they always cost more than the value of the defective goods they find
questions.explanation: Inspection detects faults but does not stop them being made, so wasted materials and labour remain. Businesses usually combine inspection with work on suppliers' processes.

questions.stem: Global sourcing in the supply chain means:
options: hiring staff only from the local community
obtaining inputs from suppliers in other countries
selling finished products to customers in overseas markets
moving the head office to another country
questions.explanation: Global sourcing is buying materials, components or services from overseas suppliers, often for lower costs or access to resources. Selling overseas is exporting.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of global sourcing?
options: easier monitoring of suppliers' working conditions
access to lower-cost inputs or materials not available locally
shorter lead times because suppliers are always closer to the factory
complete protection from changes in the Australian dollar
questions.explanation: Overseas suppliers may offer lower costs, specialist skills or materials unavailable in Australia. Distance usually lengthens lead times and makes monitoring harder, and exchange rate movements add risk.

questions.stem: A Newcastle electronics firm sources all its components from one overseas supplier. A port strike there halts shipments for a month. Which disadvantage of global sourcing does this show?
options: lower product quality because overseas suppliers lack any standards
higher company tax because imported components are taxed as profit
greater supply chain risk from long distances and reliance on one source
higher labour costs because overseas wages are always above Australian wages
questions.explanation: Long, complex supply chains are exposed to disruptions such as strikes, shipping delays and natural disasters, especially with a single supplier. Using several suppliers or holding safety stock reduces this risk.

questions.stem: Outsourcing in the supply chain involves:
options: moving a business's own employees to a new site within Australia
selling finished goods through an independent retailer
contracting another business to perform a process or produce a part
buying another business so that all of its processes are brought in-house
questions.explanation: Outsourcing hands a process, such as manufacturing a component, logistics or payroll, to an external specialist. Buying another business brings processes in-house, the opposite.

questions.stem: A Wollongong craft brewery outsources its canning to a specialist firm. Which is the most likely advantage?
options: lower costs from employing more of its own staff
access to specialist equipment without buying it
complete control over every step of production
no risk of the supplier missing a delivery date
questions.explanation: Outsourcing lets the brewery use a specialist's expertise and equipment without a large capital outlay, so it can focus on brewing. It reduces control and relies on the supplier's reliability.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of outsourcing part of the supply chain?
options: more staff needed for the outsourced task
less control over quality and timing
greater need for specialist equipment
higher capital costs for new machinery
questions.explanation: When another firm performs the task, the business depends on that firm's quality, reliability and confidentiality. Outsourcing usually reduces, not increases, the need for its own equipment and staff.

questions.stem: A business outsources its customer call centre to cut costs. Complaints about service rise sharply. Which evaluation is most valid?
options: cost savings may be outweighed by damage to reputation and lost customers
outsourcing always raises service quality, so complaints must have another cause
outsourcing has no effect on customers, because only internal staff are affected
cost savings prove the decision was correct, whatever happens to complaints
questions.explanation: Outsourcing decisions must weigh lower costs against risks to quality and reputation, since the outsourced provider deals directly with customers. Lost customers can cost more than the savings.

questions.stem: A Hunter Valley grower supplies fresh berries to supermarkets. Which logistical consideration is most important?
options: refrigerated transport and fast delivery because the product is perishable
secure storage for several months to wait for prices to rise
bulk shipping by sea to reduce the cost of each tonne of fruit carried overseas
flat-pack packaging so that more units fit into each truck
questions.explanation: Perishable products need temperature control and short transit times, often called a cold chain. Long storage or slow sea freight would spoil the berries.

questions.stem: An online retailer sells direct to customers across NSW, while a rival sells only through supermarket chains. How do their logistics most likely differ?
options: neither needs logistics, because the customer or supermarket collects the goods
the online retailer sends many small parcels to homes; the rival ships bulk loads to distribution centres
the online retailer ships bulk loads to distribution centres; the rival sends many small parcels to homes
both must use refrigerated trucks, because all retail products are perishable
questions.explanation: Logistics depend on the distribution channel: direct-to-consumer selling means many small home deliveries, while selling through retailers means larger shipments to their warehouses. Most retail products are not perishable.

questions.stem: A Sydney business makes high-value, fragile medical instruments. Which logistical choice best suits these product characteristics?
options: storage in the open air to keep the instruments cool and well ventilated
protective packaging, tracked and insured freight, and careful handling
the cheapest bulk freight available, as speed and handling do not matter
refrigerated trucks only, because all medical products are perishable
questions.explanation: Fragile, valuable goods need secure packaging, tracking and insurance to prevent damage and loss, even at a higher freight cost. Refrigeration is needed only for temperature-sensitive products.

questions.stem: A Thredbo ski hire shop expects demand to peak in July. Which response uses flexible labour to manage the fluctuation?
options: buying extra skis in summer when prices are low
raising hire prices on the busiest weekends
closing the shop on weekdays all year round
hiring casual staff for the winter season
questions.explanation: Flexible labour, such as casuals, overtime or seasonal staff, lets the business match staffing to demand. Buying extra skis is an inventory response, and raising peak prices is a pricing response.

questions.stem: A Sydney cinema charges less for sessions on Tuesday afternoons than on Saturday nights. This manages fluctuations in demand through:
options: pricing, to shift some customers to quieter times
inventory, by storing seats for busier sessions
flexible labour, by hiring more staff on Saturdays
outsourcing, by using another cinema's screens
questions.explanation: Lower off-peak prices encourage customers to move from busy to quiet times, smoothing demand. A service such as a cinema seat cannot be stored as inventory.

questions.stem: Why can a manufacturer use inventory to manage seasonal demand when a hairdressing salon cannot?
options: goods can be made in quiet periods and stored, but services cannot be stored
salons are not allowed by law to hold any stock on their premises
manufacturers face no storage costs at all, whereas salons always face high rents
services have steady demand all year, so inventory is never needed
questions.explanation: Manufactured goods can be built up as stock before a peak, while services are produced and consumed at the same time, so salons rely on flexible labour or pricing. Holding stock does involve storage costs.

questions.stem: Partly assembled bicycles waiting to have wheels fitted are an example of:
options: non-current assets
work in process inventory
inventory of materials
finished goods inventory
questions.explanation: Work in process is inventory that has started but not finished production. Raw tubes and components not yet used are materials, and completed bikes ready for sale are finished goods.

questions.stem: Which is finished goods inventory for a furniture maker?
options: the saws and sanders used in the workshop
completed dining tables waiting to be delivered
timber and screws in the storeroom
chairs that are glued together but not yet painted or sealed
questions.explanation: Finished goods are completed products ready to sell. Timber and screws are materials, half-made chairs are work in process, and tools are equipment, not inventory.

questions.stem: For a bakery, flour and sugar held in the storeroom are an example of:
options: finished goods inventory
non-current assets
inventory of materials
work in process inventory
questions.explanation: Materials are inputs that have not yet entered production. Dough that is proving would be work in process, and baked loaves ready to sell are finished goods.

questions.stem: A Penrith bike maker values its inventory at $50,000 of materials, $30,000 of work in process and $70,000 of finished goods. Sales slow sharply. Which category is most at risk of building up?
options: finished goods, as completed bikes wait longer to be sold
materials, as suppliers stop delivering any more parts
work in process, as finished bikes are taken apart again
none, because inventory levels do not respond to sales
questions.explanation: When sales slow, completed products are not sold as quickly, so finished goods stock rises and ties up cash. The business may respond by cutting production, which reduces materials and work in process over time.

questions.stem: A just-in-case approach to inventory involves:
options: ordering materials only at the moment they are needed for production
selling all finished goods before buying any new materials
outsourcing storage so that no stock is ever held on site
holding extra stock as a buffer against delays or rises in demand
questions.explanation: Just-in-case holds safety stock so production and sales can continue if supplies are delayed or demand jumps. Ordering only as needed is just-in-time.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of a just-in-case approach?
options: high storage costs and the risk of stock becoming obsolete or spoiling
a high risk of production stopping when a single delivery is late
a need for very reliable suppliers who are able to deliver several times a day
an inability to respond to a sudden increase in customer demand
questions.explanation: Holding large buffers ties up cash and space and risks waste. Vulnerability to late deliveries is a disadvantage of just-in-time, not just-in-case.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of just-in-time inventory management?
options: less need to communicate closely with suppliers
lower storage costs and less cash tied up in stock
a large buffer of stock if a supplier is late
the ability to meet any sudden rise in demand
questions.explanation: Just-in-time keeps stock to a minimum, cutting storage, insurance and waste and freeing cash for other uses. It removes the buffer, so it needs very close coordination with suppliers.

questions.stem: Just-in-time inventory management is most likely to succeed when a business has:
options: a large warehouse and plenty of spare cash to hold stock
one overseas supplier with long and variable shipping times
reliable nearby suppliers and steady, predictable demand
unreliable suppliers and sudden swings in customer demand
questions.explanation: Just-in-time depends on frequent, dependable deliveries and demand that can be forecast accurately. Unreliable or distant suppliers make stockouts likely.

questions.stem: During a global shipping crisis, a JIT car-parts maker halts production, while a rival using just-in-case keeps supplying customers. Which conclusion is most valid?
options: the JIT firm's problem was caused by poor quality control inspections
JIT lowers holding costs but increases vulnerability to supply disruptions
JIT always produces lower profits than just-in-case in every possible situation
just-in-case has no costs, so every business should hold maximum stock
questions.explanation: The two methods trade off cost against risk: JIT saves storage and cash but leaves no buffer, while just-in-case protects supply at a higher holding cost. Neither is best in all situations.

questions.stem: Which business is best suited to just-in-time inventory management?
options: a hardware store in a remote town with fortnightly deliveries
a toy importer whose sales triple in the weeks before Christmas
a hospital that must never run out of essential medicines
a sandwich bar using fresh bread delivered daily by a local baker
questions.explanation: Perishable inputs and a reliable local supplier with daily delivery suit JIT. Remote locations, big seasonal peaks and critical items where a stockout is unacceptable all favour holding buffer stock.

questions.stem: A florist holds only one or two days of stock. Which product characteristic best explains this?
options: perishability
low storage cost
steady demand
high durability
questions.explanation: Cut flowers deteriorate quickly, so holding large stocks would lead to waste. Perishable products push businesses towards small, frequent orders.

questions.stem: A Bathurst business sells large, bulky water tanks. Why might it hold few tanks in stock and make them to order?
options: the law prohibits businesses from storing water tanks outdoors
storage costs are high because each tank takes up a lot of space
water tanks are perishable and spoil quickly if they are stored
demand for water tanks never changes from one month to the next
questions.explanation: High storage costs, such as space for bulky items, encourage lower inventory levels. Tanks are durable, not perishable.

questions.stem: A sunscreen maker's sales triple every summer. How is this demand pattern most likely to affect its inventory management?
options: it holds the same small stock all year and accepts lost summer sales
it switches to services in summer, since goods cannot be stored
it stops all production in summer to avoid storing excess stock
it builds up finished goods stock in winter and spring ahead of the peak
questions.explanation: Predictable seasonal fluctuations can be met by producing steadily and storing finished goods before the peak, avoiding the cost of huge capacity used only in summer.

questions.stem: A Tamworth meat processor uses its own trucks to deliver to butchers, but contracts a cleaning company to sanitise its plant each night. Which statement is correct?
options: delivery is outsourced, while cleaning is kept in-house
both tasks are global sourcing, as they involve suppliers
neither task is part of the business's supply chain
cleaning is outsourced, while delivery is kept in-house
questions.explanation: Outsourcing means contracting an external business to perform a process, as with the nightly cleaning. Using its own trucks keeps logistics in-house. Global sourcing refers to obtaining inputs from overseas suppliers.

questions.stem: An Australian furniture retailer switches from a supplier in Asia to one in regional NSW, even though unit costs rise by 8%. Which reason would best justify the decision?
options: shorter lead times and more reliable supply reduce stockouts and holding costs
local suppliers are required by law for all furniture sold in Australia
a higher unit cost always leads to a higher profit margin for the furniture retailer
global sourcing cannot provide any cost savings for furniture retailers
questions.explanation: A local supplier can deliver faster and more reliably, so the retailer can hold less safety stock and lose fewer sales, which may outweigh the higher unit cost. There is no legal requirement to buy furniture locally.

questions.stem: The Australian Government raises a tariff on an imported component used by a NSW manufacturer. What is the most likely effect on its operations?
options: the business's selling price must stay fixed by law for one year
the cost of the imported input rises, so it may switch to a local supplier
the cost of the imported input falls, so it buys more from overseas
the business must stop all imports, because tariffs ban foreign goods outright
questions.explanation: A tariff is a tax on imports, so it raises the cost of overseas inputs and may make local suppliers more competitive. Tariffs make imports dearer but do not ban them.

questions.stem: A free trade agreement between Australia and another country is most likely to affect a business's supply chain by:
options: requiring the business to outsource production to that country
removing all quality and safety standards on goods traded
lowering tariffs, which can make sourcing from that country cheaper
raising tariffs, which makes imports from that country more expensive
questions.explanation: Free trade agreements reduce or remove tariffs and other barriers between member countries, so sourcing from them can become cheaper. Product safety standards still apply.

questions.stem: A Sydney phone retailer takes back customers' old phones so that their materials can be recovered. This environmental consideration relates to the product's:
options: by-products
lead time
end-of-life
inputs
questions.explanation: End-of-life considerations deal with what happens to a product after use, such as take-back, recycling and safe disposal. Inputs are the materials used, and by-products are the waste created during production.

questions.stem: Which is an environmental consideration about the inputs to a product?
options: reusing waste created during the production process
setting a lower price to clear excess finished goods
choosing recycled or sustainably sourced materials
taking back used products from customers for recycling
questions.explanation: Inputs are the materials and energy that go into production, so sourcing recycled or certified sustainable materials addresses them. Take-back schemes concern end-of-life, and reusing production waste concerns by-products.

questions.stem: A paper mill captures wood waste from its production and burns it to generate electricity for the mill. This environmental consideration relates to:
options: the inputs bought from overseas suppliers
the trade policies of the government
the by-products of the production process
the end-of-life of the paper products
questions.explanation: By-products are outputs other than the main product, such as waste, emissions and offcuts; reusing them reduces waste and costs. End-of-life concerns the product after customers have used it.

questions.stem: A clothing brand finds that one of its overseas suppliers uses forced labour. Which response best reflects ethical global sourcing?
options: raise retail prices so that customers share the cost of the problem
investigate, require the supplier to fix the practices or end the contract
keep the supplier, since its practices are legal under Australian law
keep the supplier but stop publishing any information about it
questions.explanation: Ethical sourcing means taking responsibility for conditions in the supply chain, acting to remedy abuses and being transparent. The Modern Slavery Act 2018 (Cth) requires large entities to report on modern slavery risks in their operations and supply chains.

questions.stem: Under the Modern Slavery Act 2018 (Cth), large entities must:
options: buy all of their inputs from suppliers based within Australia
pay every overseas worker in their supply chain the Australian minimum wage
obtain government approval before using any overseas supplier
report on the risks of modern slavery in their operations and supply chains
questions.explanation: The Act requires reporting entities to publish modern slavery statements describing the risks in their operations and supply chains and the actions taken to address them. It does not ban overseas suppliers.
